newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: HORSE RACING-AUSTRALIA IN A FLAP OVER PHAR LAP.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-AUSTRALIA IN A FLAP OVER PHAR LAP.

text.p: Sporting groups, politicians and even a casino are brawling over the scattered remains of Australia's most famous racehorse, Phar Lap, whose mysterious death 65 years ago shocked a nation and spawned fevered conspiracy theories.

The local government running the national capital, where Phar Lap's abnormally large heart is stored, said on Friday it wanted the big red gelding's stuffed hide back from the southern city of Melbourne and his skeleton returned from his birthplace in New Zealand.
But Melbourne's Crown Casino, the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the Victorian Racing Club are also scrambling for a piece of the action surrounding racing's wonder horse of the 1930s.

The squabble was prompted by news that the stuffed hide, one of the most popular exhibits in the Victorian state museum in Melbourne, may go into storage for two years while the state builds a new museum.
Then Melbourne's high-rolling Crown Casino offered to put the glass-eyed hide, stretched over a fibreglass and papier-mache frame, in a special exhibit.
"We'd love to have Phar Lap down here -- 12 to 14 million people go through the casino every year, which is a bit more than the museum," said casino boss Lloyd Williams.

But Canberra government chief minister Kate Carnell said the legendary galloper, known as Big Red, was a national icon and his remains should be re-united in a soon-to-be-built national museum in Canberra.
"I think we should put an end to such fights once and for all by declaring that Phar Lap is a national icon and should rest in peace at the National Museum of Australia," she said.
Victorian state leader Jeff Kennett insists Phar Lap's skin is too fragile to go anywhere.
"It has been at its current location for so long there are very real curatorial concerns that if it was moved ... we could actually destroy the exhibit," he said.
And officials at the Museum of New Zealand in Wellington were adamant that the horse's skeleton would be one of the museum's major exhibits when it opens next year.
The hugely-popular Phar Lap was virtually unbeatable in the early 1930s, winning 37 races including the 1930 Melbourne Cup, Australia's richest race.
The towering gelding died of unknown causes in California in 1932, sparking rumours about mafia nobbling and jealous American racers that resurface even now.

It is considered to be such a significant part of Australian history, that it is even ranked in some listings of the most influential Australians -- despite being a horse, and a New Zealander at that.

"Think of all the excitement over the America's Cup and the way Australians love knocking off the world, then imagine Australia in the 1930s and how powerful it would have been then, during the depression, for us to thrash America," said Victorian Museum director Graham Morris.
"He really signified our place in the world."
